distillation_scope.leaf_granularity: First-layer disease leaf for hepatic abscess caused by invasive Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites after intestinal mucosal invasion and portal venous spread. The leaf is independent of abscess side, size, rupture status, travel source, host risk group, venous thrombosis, bacterial coinfection, or treatment response.
distillation_scope.boundary_policy: Pyogenic liver abscess, acute cholangitis, acute cholecystitis, hydatid cyst, hepatic malignancy, tuberculosis, fungal liver abscess, isolated empyema, lung abscess, pericarditis, pulmonary embolism, portal vein thrombosis, and generic sepsis remain competing manifolds or complications/context. They are not appended to the disease name.
distillation_scope.ranking_note: Presentation ranking should use fever, chills, malaise, diarrhea or dysentery history, right upper quadrant or epigastric pain, referred shoulder pain, hepatomegaly, jaundice, chest or respiratory symptoms, vital signs, CBC, CRP/PCT, liver tests, albumin, INR, lactate, CT/ultrasound liver abscess morphology, solitary right-lobe tendency, left-lobe or subcapsular rupture risk, pleural/pericardial/peritoneal extension, venous thrombosis, and Entamoeba serology/PCR when available. Aspirate appearance, pathogen PCR, serology, culture results, and treatment response can be confirmatory or post-workup context depending on the testing mode.

latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Ingested Entamoeba histolytica cysts excyst in the colon, with trophozoite adherence, cytotoxic epithelial invasion, and intermittent colitis or asymptomatic carriage before hepatic spread.
Trophozoites enter the portal circulation and seed hepatic sinusoids, classically favoring the right lobe but able to involve the left lobe or multiple sites.
Amoebic cytotoxicity, hepatocyte necrosis, complement resistance, and neutrophil lysis create a necrotic inflammatory focus with few viable bacteria unless coinfection is present.
Necrotic hepatic tissue liquefies into a solitary or less often multiple cavity, often containing odorless brown anchovy-paste-like material and showing low-attenuation or ring-enhancing imaging.
Hepatic necrosis and parasite antigens drive fever, chills, tachycardia, neutrophilic leukocytosis, CRP elevation, malaise, anorexia, and sometimes sepsis-like physiology.

Subcapsular hepatic inflammation stretches Glisson capsule and irritates diaphragm, causing right upper quadrant or epigastric pain, referred shoulder pain, cough, pleuritic pain, and reactive pleural effusion.
Large, superficial, left-lobe, or delayed-treatment abscesses can breach capsule into pleural, pericardial, peritoneal, abdominal wall, subdiaphragmatic, or bronchial spaces.
Large abscess mass effect, adjacent inflammation, and local venous stasis can produce portal vein, hepatic vein, inferior vena cava thrombosis, and rarely pulmonary embolic complications.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Persistent tissue or luminal parasite burden
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Incomplete tissue amoebicide exposure, very large cavity, unrecognized rupture, or absent luminal eradication can sustain symptoms or later recurrence.
Severe systemic inflammation, rupture, bacterial coinfection, hypovolemia, or delayed source control can drive hypotension, hypoxemia, lactate rise, AKI, coagulopathy, and mortality hazard.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Invasive colonic trophozoites reach hepatic sinusoids through portal venous drainage.
Hepatic seeding initiates local trophozoite cytotoxicity and hepatocyte necrosis.
Necrotic liver tissue liquefies and coalesces into a radiographic abscess cavity.
Tissue necrosis and parasite antigens drive fever and acute-phase response.
An enlarging cavity stretches liver capsule and irritates the diaphragm.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Risk rises with large, superficial, left-lobe, subcapsular, or delayed-treated abscesses.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Cavity pressure and enzymatic tissue destruction can breach adjacent planes.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Most important with giant abscesses adjacent to portal or hepatic venous branches.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Mass effect and local inflammation cause venous stasis and thrombosis.
Pleural, pericardial, peritoneal, or abdominal wall rupture can rapidly increase physiologic stress and source-control need.
Persistent viable parasite burden sustains fever and inflammatory markers.
High systemic inflammation can produce vasodilation, capillary leak, and hypoperfusion.
ALA commonly presents with subjective fever.
Pyrogenic cytokines raise measured temperature.
High fever and inflammatory bursts produce chills or rigors.
Fever, pain, and inflammation drive tachycardia.
Neutrophilic leukocytosis is common even when abscess cultures are sterile.
ALA commonly produces neutrophil predominance.
Hepatic acute-phase response elevates CRP.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Often lower than severe bacterial sepsis but may rise with extensive inflammation or bacterial coinfection.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Severe systemic inflammation can elevate procalcitonin.

Inflammation and liver capsule pain reduce appetite.
Colonic amoebiasis may precede or accompany hepatic abscess, but diarrhea can be absent.
Capsular stretch commonly causes right upper quadrant pain.

Diaphragmatic irritation can refer pain to the shoulder through the phrenic nerve.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: More likely with diaphragmatic irritation, pleural reaction, or thoracic rupture.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Diaphragmatic and pleural irritation can trigger cough.
Reactive effusion or true rupture may accompany subdiaphragmatic inflammation.
Hepatic inflammation and necrosis can mildly or moderately elevate AST.
Hepatic inflammation and necrosis can mildly or moderately elevate ALT.
Space-occupying abscess and cholestatic irritation often raise alkaline phosphatase.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Jaundice is variable and more likely with large, central, or complicated abscess.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Inflammation and mass effect can produce cholestasis.
Inflammation and chronic illness lower albumin.
The disease requires a hepatic abscess cavity.
Ongoing necrosis and liquefaction enlarge the cavity.
ALA is classically solitary and right-lobe predominant because of portal flow anatomy.
Amoebic cytolysis produces odorless brown necrotic aspirate when sampled.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Culture can become positive with bacterial coinfection or prior instrumentation.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Uncomplicated ALA usually has negative bacterial cultures.
Rupture begins with capsular or subcapsular extension.
Transdiaphragmatic extension indicates thoracic rupture.
Rupture can seed pleura or lung and cause effusion, empyema, or pulmonary amoebiasis.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Mainly with left-lobe or superior subcapsular abscess.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Left-lobe abscess can rupture into pericardium and cause tamponade.
Adjacent inflammation and compression can thrombose portal branches.
Venous thrombosis and inflammation can elevate D-dimer.
Large abscesses can contribute to venous thromboembolic risk, though causality is variable.
Severe inflammation or rupture can produce hypotension.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: More likely with pleural rupture, empyema, PE, ARDS, or large effusion.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Thoracic complications and shock impair oxygenation.
Hypoperfusion and adrenergic stress increase lactate.
Severe illness can produce AKI.
Shock, hypoxemia, rupture, and organ dysfunction raise short-term mortality risk.
Peritoneal, pleural, and pericardial rupture are major causes of death in complicated ALA.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Fever and CRP are correlated outputs of systemic inflammation, not direct causes of each other.
Leukocytosis in ALA is usually neutrophil-predominant.
Large abscesses are more likely to need diagnostic aspiration or therapeutic drainage.
Increasing diameter and tension raise rupture risk.
Left-lobe ALA is anatomically closer to the pericardium.
Diaphragmatic rupture can rapidly increase pleural fluid.
Large effusions and empyema reduce lung expansion and oxygenation.
Venous thrombosis contributes to fibrin turnover and D-dimer elevation.
Observed thrombosis indicates high near-term thrombosis hazard and persistence risk.
Hyperlactatemia reflects hypoperfusion and severe systemic illness.
Low MAP increases short-term mortality risk.
Adequate drainage of ruptured or nonresponding collections lowers complication and mortality pressure.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Positive serology supports ALA as the treatment target.
PCR confirmation supports active Entamoeba burden.
Severe hepatic dysfunction can increase nitroimidazole toxicity and monitoring needs.

failure_modes: Ruptured or very large collection needing drainage
No luminal eradication with later recurrence

side_effects.interpretation: Clinically significant hepatotoxicity is uncommon but monitoring is needed in severe liver disease.

treatments.context_specific_role: Rapidly lowers hepatic trophozoite activity and systemic inflammatory drift when ALA is plausible or confirmed.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Tinidazole can be used when metronidazole tolerance or dosing is problematic.
Nitroimidazole exposure requires caution in severe hepatic impairment.

failure_modes: No luminal agent after tissue therapy
Ruptured collection without drainage when needed
treatments.context_specific_role: Alternative nitroimidazole tissue therapy for ALA.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Stool positivity indicates intestinal carriage, but luminal therapy is relevant even when stool tests are negative.
Aminoglycoside-class luminal therapy may need renal caution despite poor absorption.

failure_modes: Used without tissue amoebicide for hepatic disease
No intestinal carriage but persistent hepatic source dominates symptoms

side_effects.interpretation: Luminal agents can cause gastrointestinal side effects.

treatments.context_specific_role: Eradicates intestinal cyst/carriage compartment after tissue therapy and reduces recurrence pressure.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Luminal agent selection depends on pregnancy and local availability.
Hepatic disease can affect tolerability and monitoring.

failure_modes: Used without tissue amoebicide for active liver abscess
treatments.context_specific_role: Alternative luminal eradication pathway when paromomycin is unsuitable or unavailable.

treatments.drug: Image-guided liver abscess aspiration or catheter drainage

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Drainage is more consequential when the cavity is large, tense, or diagnostically uncertain.
No safe window or poorly liquefied contents reduce procedural benefit.
Coagulopathy or unsafe route increases procedural risk.

side_effects.interpretation: Instrumentation can rarely introduce or reveal bacterial superinfection.

treatments.context_specific_role: Diagnostic and therapeutic decompression when abscess is large, left-lobe, ruptured, nonresponding, or diagnosis is uncertain.

treatments.drug: Thoracentesis, chest tube drainage, or VATS decortication

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Large effusions produce greater respiratory benefit from drainage.
Loculated collections may need catheter drainage, fibrinolysis, or VATS.
Pleural procedures carry bleeding risk.

side_effects.interpretation: Thoracic drainage or VATS can bleed or cause air leak.

treatments.context_specific_role: Controls pleural space complication and improves oxygenation when ALA ruptures into the thorax.

treatments.drug: Broad-spectrum antibacterial coverage while pyogenic coinfection is unresolved

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Antibacterial benefit depends on bacterial coinfection or uncertain pyogenic abscess.
Negative bacterial culture after adequate sampling lowers antibacterial causal effect.

side_effects.interpretation: Broad antibiotics can increase C. difficile risk.

treatments.context_specific_role: Covers bacterial liver abscess or coinfection uncertainty until microbiology and clinical course clarify the causal field.

treatments.drug: Therapeutic anticoagulation for documented venous thrombosis

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Portal thrombosis is one context where anticoagulation may reduce persistence or extension.
Observed PE gives direct anticoagulation indication if bleeding risk permits.
Active bleeding, high-risk procedures, or coagulopathy can preclude anticoagulation.

failure_modes: Need for urgent drainage with high bleeding risk
Thrombus caused by uncontrolled source not yet treated

side_effects.interpretation: Anticoagulation increases bleeding risk, especially around drainage.

treatments.context_specific_role: Adjunct for documented portal, hepatic, caval, or pulmonary thromboembolic complications after balancing procedure and bleeding risks.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Hemodynamic support is relevant when hypotension or hypoperfusion is present.
Supportive hemodynamics do not remove the hepatic or thoracic source.

treatments.context_specific_role: Temporizes shock physiology while anti-amoebic therapy and drainage reshape the causal field.

present.trajectory_modulation: Epidemiologic enrichment for invasive ALA without a specific axis signature.
Raises prior probability of Entamoeba colonization and later ALA, even if travel was remote.
Raises Entamoeba transmission risk in nonendemic settings.
Raises invasive amebiasis risk and complicated abscess morbidity; background glucose/HbA1c should not be explained by ALA itself.
Raises risk of invasive disease and atypical presentations; CD4-preserved HIV may still have ALA.
Can worsen immune response, hypoalbuminemia, and pleuropulmonary complication risk.
Raises rupture, pericardial, pleural, abdominal wall extension, and source-control need.
Sustains trophozoite activity, abscess expansion, rupture risk, and mortality hazard.
Raises need for antibacterial bridge and makes fever/PCT/culture behavior more pyogenic-like.

supportive_care: Use contrast CT or high-quality ultrasound to define abscess size, lobe, number, liquefaction, subcapsular extension, rupture, pleural/pericardial/peritoneal spread, and safe drainage route.
Send E. histolytica serology and, when material is available, PCR or antigen testing from stool, abscess aspirate, pleural fluid, or relevant specimens; microscopy alone is insensitive.
Send abscess, blood, and pleural cultures when sampled because pyogenic abscess or bacterial coinfection changes treatment context.
Trend temperature, heart rate, respiratory status, WBC/ANC, CRP, liver tests, albumin, INR, creatinine, lactate, D-dimer when thrombosis is suspected, and oxygenation when thoracic spread is present.
Reassess early with imaging and procedural teams if fever, pain, hypoxemia, inflammatory markers, or cavity size fail to improve after tissue amoebicide or if rupture is suspected.

Coordinate infectious diseases, interventional radiology, hepatobiliary surgery, and thoracic/cardiac teams when the abscess is large, left-lobe, ruptured, loculated, near pericardium, or associated with pleural/pericardial collections.
Give luminal eradication after tissue therapy unless a contraindication or local availability issue requires another plan.
Balance anticoagulation against drainage and bleeding risk when portal, hepatic, caval, or pulmonary thromboembolic complications are documented.
Use standard supportive care for shock or respiratory failure while anti-amoebic therapy and drainage address the causal field.
Arrange follow-up imaging because radiographic cavity resolution may lag clinical response, and monitor for recurrence when luminal treatment was delayed or incomplete.
quality_notes: No fields encode first-line, preference, guideline status, or indication strength; treatment ranking is left to runtime outcome simulation.

New amoebic pathogen axes are pathogen-confirmation axes, not case-specific ranking patches. Pyogenic liver abscess, empyema, pulmonary embolism, portal thrombosis, and pericarditis leaves should retain their own shared clinical axes and only lack Entamoeba-specific microbiology when medically absent.

Hepatic abscess morphology is disease-owned for this leaf to avoid double-counting pyogenic liver abscess axes while allowing shared generic source-control, pleural, thrombosis, and sepsis physiology axes.
